Part 1: Big Data Fundamentals & Architecture¶

The 5 V's of Big Data¶

V Meaning Example
Volume Massive amount of data Petabytes of log data, social media posts
Velocity Speed at which data is generated & processed Real-time clickstreams, IoT sensor feeds
Variety Different types and formats of data Structured (SQL), semi-structured (JSON), unstructured (images)
Veracity Accuracy and trustworthiness of data Noisy sensor data, incomplete records, duplicates
Value Business insights derived from data Customer churn prediction, fraud detection

Distributed Computing Concepts¶

Source: CAP Theorem — Wikipedia

Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling¶

Aspect Vertical (Scale Up) Horizontal (Scale Out)
Method Add more CPU/RAM to one machine Add more machines
Cost Expensive (bigger hardware) Cheaper (commodity hardware)
Limit Physical hardware limit Virtually unlimited
Fault Tolerance Single point of failure Redundancy across nodes
Big Data? Not suitable Preferred approach

Data Architecture Patterns¶

Pattern Description Use Case
Data Lake Store raw data in any format (schema-on-read) Exploration, ML, cheap storage
Data Warehouse Store structured, cleaned data (schema-on-write) BI, reporting, analytics
Data Lakehouse Lake + warehouse capabilities (ACID, SQL, governance) Modern unified platform
Data Mesh Decentralized data ownership by domain teams Large organizations, autonomy
Data Fabric AI-driven data management across all environments Multi-cloud, auto-discovery

Batch vs Stream Processing¶

Aspect Batch Processing Stream Processing
Latency Minutes to hours Milliseconds to seconds
Data Bounded (finite dataset) Unbounded (continuous)
Tools Spark, MapReduce, Hive Kafka Streams, Flink, Spark Streaming
Use Case ETL, reporting, backfill Fraud detection, real-time dashboards
Complexity Simpler to debug/test Harder (state, ordering, late data)

Lambda vs Kappa Architecture¶

Lambda Architecture      Kappa Architecture

Source: Hazelcast — Lambda Architecture

Two code paths → complex      One code path → simpler

Data Serialization Formats¶

Format Type Schema Splittable Best For
Parquet Columnar Embedded Analytics, Spark default
ORC Columnar Embedded Hive optimized, ACID
Avro Row-based Embedded Streaming, schema evolution
JSON Row-based None APIs, semi-structured
CSV Row-based None Simple exchange, legacy

Schema-on-Read vs Schema-on-Write¶

Aspect Schema-on-Read Schema-on-Write
When schema applied At query time At write/load time
Where Data lake Data warehouse
Flexibility High (any format) Low (strict schema)
Data quality Lower (raw data) Higher (validated)
Tools Spark, Presto, Athena RDBMS, Snowflake, Redshift

ETL vs ELT¶

Aspect ETL ELT
Transform Before loading After loading
Where ETL tool (Informatica, Talend) In warehouse/lake (SQL, Spark)
Storage Warehouse only Lake + warehouse
Modern? Traditional (on-prem) Modern (cloud-native)
Scalability Limited by ETL tool Scales with cloud compute

Big Data Fundamentals — Interview Questions¶

# Question Keywords Answer
1 What is Big Data? What are the 5 V's? Big Data, 5V • Massive datasets too large for traditional systems
• Volume: petabytes of data
• Velocity: speed of generation (real-time streams)
• Variety: structured, semi-structured, unstructured
• Veracity: data accuracy/trustworthiness
• Value: business insights derived
2 How does distributed computing solve Big Data challenges? Distributed, parallel • Splits data across multiple machines (nodes)
• Each node processes a portion in parallel
• Scales horizontally by adding more nodes
• Fault tolerance via replication and redundancy
3 Horizontal vs vertical scaling — why does Big Data favor horizontal? Scaling, horizontal • Vertical: add more CPU/RAM to one machine (has limits)
• Horizontal: add more machines (commodity hardware)
• Horizontal is cheaper and virtually unlimited
• Big Data needs horizontal for fault tolerance and scale
4 Explain the CAP theorem. CAP, distributed • Consistency: all nodes see same data simultaneously
• Availability: every request gets a response
• Partition Tolerance: system works despite network failures
• Can only guarantee 2 of 3 (CP: HBase; AP: Cassandra)
5 OLTP vs OLAP systems? OLTP, OLAP • OLTP: transactional, row-oriented, low latency (MySQL, PostgreSQL)
• OLAP: analytical, columnar, batch aggregations (Redshift, BigQuery)
• OLTP for writes; OLAP for reads/analytics
• ETL/ELT feeds data from OLTP → OLAP
6 Data lake vs data warehouse? Lake, warehouse • Data lake: raw data, any format, schema-on-read, cheap storage
• Data warehouse: structured, cleaned, schema-on-write, optimized for BI
• Lake for exploration/ML; warehouse for reporting
• Modern trend: lakehouse combines both
7 What is a data lakehouse? Why popular? Lakehouse • Combines data lake flexibility with warehouse reliability
• ACID transactions on open formats (Delta, Iceberg)
• Supports both BI/SQL and ML workloads
• One copy of data serves all use cases — lower cost
8 Batch vs stream processing — when each? Batch, streaming • Batch: process collected data at intervals (hourly/daily)
• Stream: process data in real-time as it arrives
• Batch for ETL, reporting; stream for fraud detection, alerts
• Stream is more complex (state, ordering, late data)
9 Lambda architecture — what problems does it solve? Lambda, architecture • Batch layer: complete, accurate view (high latency)
• Speed layer: real-time, approximate view (low latency)
• Serving layer: merged results for queries
• Problem: two codebases to maintain (complex)
10 Kappa architecture — how does it simplify Lambda? Kappa, streaming • Streaming-only architecture (no separate batch layer)
• Everything is treated as a stream
• Replay capability for reprocessing historical data
• Simpler: one codebase, one processing path
11 Why is data partitioning critical for performance? Partitioning, performance • Divides data into smaller chunks across nodes
• Enables parallel processing (each partition on separate core)
• Reduces data scanned per query (partition pruning)
• Too few partitions → under-utilization; too many → overhead
12 Data replication — tradeoffs? Replication, tradeoff • Copies data across multiple nodes for fault tolerance
• Higher replication = more durability, more storage cost
• Consistency vs availability tradeoff (CAP theorem)
• Default replication factor: 3 in HDFS
13 Sharding vs partitioning? Sharding, partition • Partitioning: dividing data within a single system (e.g., by date)
• Sharding: distributing data across multiple independent databases
• Sharding enables horizontal scaling of databases
• Partition is logical; shard is physical distribution
14 Eventual consistency vs strong consistency? Consistency, eventual • Eventual: all replicas converge to same value over time (Cassandra, DynamoDB)
• Strong: reads always see the latest write (HBase, ZooKeeper)
• Eventual = higher availability, lower latency
• Strong = guaranteed correctness, higher latency
15 Fault tolerance in distributed systems? Fault tolerance • Ability to continue operating despite node failures
• Replication: data copied to multiple nodes
• Lineage: Spark recomputes lost partitions from DAG
• Checkpointing: periodic snapshots to durable storage
16 Compare Avro, Parquet, ORC, and JSON for Big Data. File format, compare • Parquet: columnar, best for analytics (Spark default)
• ORC: columnar, Hive-optimized, ACID support
• Avro: row-based, great schema evolution, good for streaming
• JSON: human-readable, no compression, slow for analytics
17 Why is Parquet preferred for analytics? Parquet, columnar • Columnar storage: reads only needed columns
• Excellent compression (Snappy, ZSTD)
• Predicate pushdown: skip irrelevant row groups
• Native support in Spark, Hive, Presto, Athena
18 Columnar vs row storage — why columnar for analytics? Columnar, row • Row: entire row stored together (good for OLTP, full-row reads)
• Columnar: each column stored separately (good for aggregations)
• Columnar compresses better (similar values together)
• Analytics queries typically scan few columns over many rows
19 Schema-on-read vs schema-on-write? Schema, read, write • Schema-on-read: apply schema when reading (data lake)
• Schema-on-write: enforce schema when writing (warehouse)
• Read: more flexible, faster ingestion
• Write: better data quality, stricter validation
20 ETL vs ELT — when each? ETL, ELT • ETL: transform before load (traditional, on-prem tools)
• ELT: load raw → transform in warehouse/lake (modern, cloud)
• ELT leverages cloud compute (Spark, SQL engines)
• ELT dominant in cloud data engineering
21 What is a data pipeline? Key components? Pipeline, components • Series of steps: extract → transform → load → validate
• Components: source, ingestion, processing, storage, orchestration
• Must be: idempotent, monitored, fault-tolerant
• Tools: Airflow (orchestration), Spark (processing), S3/ADLS (storage)
22 What is data governance? Why important? Governance • Policies for data quality, security, privacy, compliance
• Ensures consistent, accurate, trustworthy data across org
• Required for: GDPR, HIPAA, SOX compliance
• Tools: Unity Catalog, Purview, DataHub, Collibra
23 What is data lineage? How to track it? Lineage, tracking • Tracks data flow from source → transformations → destination
• Answers: where did this data come from? What changed it?
• Tools: Unity Catalog, OpenLineage, Purview, DataHub
• Critical for debugging, compliance, impact analysis
24 Metadata management in Big Data? Metadata • Data about data: schemas, stats, lineage, ownership
• Technical metadata (column types, row counts)
• Business metadata (descriptions, owners, tags)
• Tools: Hive Metastore, Glue Catalog, Unity Catalog
25 How to handle data quality in Big Data? Data quality • Dimensions: accuracy, completeness, timeliness, consistency
• Implement validation checks at each pipeline stage
• Tools: Great Expectations, Soda, dbt tests, Deequ
• Quarantine bad data, don't propagate downstream
26 What is data cataloging? Tools? Catalog, tools • Searchable inventory of datasets and metadata
• Makes data discoverable across an organization
• Tools: DataHub, Amundsen, Unity Catalog, Purview, Glue Catalog
• Auto-crawl databases, tag sensitive columns
27 Idempotency — why crucial in data pipelines? Idempotent • Re-running operation produces same result (no duplicates)
• Implement: MERGE/upsert instead of INSERT
• Use execution_date, not current timestamp
• Enables: safe retries, backfilling, error recovery
28 What is backpressure in stream processing? Backpressure • When producer sends data faster than consumer can process
• Can cause: OOM errors, dropped messages, crashes
• Handle: rate limiting, buffering (Kafka), auto-scaling
• Kafka handles via consumer lag; Flink via credit-based flow control
29 SQL-based vs code-based approach for data processing? SQL, code, decide • SQL: declarative, familiar to analysts, good for structured data
• Code (PySpark/Python): flexible, complex logic, ML integration
• SQL for: transforms, aggregations, reporting
• Code for: ML pipelines, custom logic, complex ETL
30 What is a splittable vs non-splittable compression codec? Compression, splittable • Splittable: can be read in parallel (Snappy, LZO, ZSTD blocks)
• Non-splittable: must read entire file sequentially (Gzip)
• Splittable preferred for distributed processing (MapReduce, Spark)
• Non-splittable = single mapper bottleneck

Part 2: Hadoop Ecosystem¶

Hadoop Overview¶

Apache Hadoop is an open-source framework for distributed storage and processing of large datasets on clusters of commodity hardware. The core ecosystem:

Source: GeeksforGeeks — Hadoop Ecosystem

HDFS Architecture¶

Component Role Details
NameNode Master — metadata manager Stores file→block mapping, permissions, replication info. Single point of failure (use HA mode)
DataNode Worker — data storage Stores actual data blocks, sends heartbeats to NameNode
Secondary NameNode Checkpoint helper Merges edit logs with fsimage periodically (NOT a hot standby)
Block Storage unit Default 128 MB; each file split into blocks
Replication Fault tolerance Default factor = 3 (rack-aware placement)
HDFS Read/Write Flow¶

WRITE: Client → NameNode (get block locations) → Client → DataNode1 → DataNode2 → DataNode3 (pipeline replication) → Pipeline ACK → Client confirms

READ: Client → NameNode (get block locations) → Client → nearest DataNode (rack-aware)

YARN Architecture¶

Component Role
ResourceManager Global resource scheduler — allocates containers
NodeManager Per-node agent — manages containers on that machine
ApplicationMaster Per-app coordinator — requests resources from RM
Container Allocation unit — CPU + memory combination

MapReduce Flow¶

Input → Split → Map Phase → Shuffle & Sort → Reduce Phase → Output

Map Phase Shuffle & Sort Reduce Phase
Produces key-value pairs Groups by key Aggregation
Parallel execution Network I/O Parallel execution

Common HDFS Commands¶

Command Description
hdfs dfs -ls / List root directory
hdfs dfs -put local.txt /data/ Upload file to HDFS
hdfs dfs -get /data/file.txt . Download file from HDFS
hdfs dfs -cat /data/file.txt Print file contents
hdfs dfs -mkdir /data/new_dir Create directory
hdfs dfs -rm -r /data/old_dir Remove directory
hdfs dfs -du -h /data/ Check directory size
hdfs fsck /data/ -files -blocks File system health check

Hadoop Ecosystem — Interview Questions¶

# Question Keywords Answer
1 What is Hadoop? Core components? Hadoop, ecosystem • Open-source framework for distributed storage+processing
• Core: HDFS (storage), MapReduce (processing), YARN (resource mgmt)
• Handles petabytes on commodity hardware
• Ecosystem: Hive, Pig, HBase, Sqoop, Flume, ZooKeeper
2 What is HDFS? How does it work? HDFS, architecture • Hadoop Distributed File System for large-scale storage
• Files split into blocks (128 MB default), replicated across DataNodes
• NameNode: stores metadata (file→block mapping)
• Designed for batch processing, write-once-read-many
3 NameNode vs DataNode? NameNode, DataNode • NameNode: master — metadata, file→block map, permissions
• DataNode: worker — stores actual data blocks
• NameNode is single point of failure (use HA mode)
• DataNodes send heartbeats and block reports
4 What is the Secondary NameNode? Is it a backup? Secondary NN • NOT a backup/standby for NameNode
• Periodically merges edit logs with fsimage (checkpointing)
• Reduces NameNode startup time
• For HA, use Standby NameNode (not secondary)
5 HDFS block size — why 128 MB? Why not smaller? Block size, 128MB • Large blocks reduce metadata overhead on NameNode
• Minimize number of disk seeks
• Better network throughput (fewer connections)
• Small blocks → too many blocks → NameNode memory pressure
6 HDFS replication factor — how does rack awareness work? Replication, rack • Default replication = 3: same rack, different rack, different rack
• Rack-aware: first replica on local rack, others on remote racks
• Survives individual node AND entire rack failure
• Configurable per file: hdfs dfs -setrep -w 2 /path
7 HDFS read and write flow? HDFS, read, write • Write: client → NameNode (locations) → pipeline: DN1→DN2→DN3
• Pipeline replication with ACK propagation
• Read: client → NameNode (locations) → nearest DataNode (rack-aware)
• Data locality: process data where it resides
8 What is HDFS Federation? Federation, NameNode • Multiple NameNodes each managing a portion of namespace
• Scales NameNode horizontally (no single bottleneck)
• Each NameNode has its own namespace volume
• DataNodes are shared across all NameNodes
9 HDFS High Availability — how implemented? HA, standby • Active NameNode + Standby NameNode (hot standby)
• Shared edit log via JournalNodes (quorum-based)
• ZooKeeper handles automatic failover (ZKFC)
• Eliminates NameNode as single point of failure
10 What is YARN? Architecture? YARN, resource • Yet Another Resource Negotiator — cluster resource manager
• ResourceManager: global scheduler, allocates containers
• NodeManager: per-node agent, manages containers
• ApplicationMaster: per-application coordinator
11 YARN schedulers — Fair vs Capacity? Scheduler, fair, capacity • Fair: equal share of resources to all running apps
• Capacity: guaranteed capacity per queue (multi-tenant)
• FIFO: oldest-first (rarely used in production)
• Capacity Scheduler is default in most Hadoop distributions
12 Explain MapReduce paradigm. MapReduce, paradigm • Programming model for parallel processing
• Map phase: process input key-value pairs → intermediate pairs
• Shuffle & Sort: group by key across network
• Reduce phase: aggregate values per key → final output
13 Why is MapReduce slow compared to Spark? MapReduce, slow • Writes intermediate results to disk after every stage
• No in-memory caching between iterations
• Rigid two-phase model (map→reduce only)
• Spark uses in-memory computation and DAG optimization
14 What is a Combiner in MapReduce? Combiner, optimization • Mini-Reducer that runs on Mapper's output locally
• Reduces data transferred during shuffle phase
• Same interface as Reducer (but runs per-mapper)
• Example: word count — combine local counts before shuffle
15 InputFormat and OutputFormat in MapReduce? InputFormat, output • InputFormat: determines how input is split and read (TextInputFormat, SequenceFileInputFormat)
• OutputFormat: determines how output is written (TextOutputFormat)
• Custom InputFormat for non-standard data sources
• Controls RecordReader and RecordWriter behavior
16 What is speculative execution in Hadoop? Speculative, straggler • Hadoop launches duplicate of slow-running tasks
• First finished task's output is accepted; other is killed
• Handles hardware degradation and data skew
• Can be disabled: mapreduce.map.speculative=false
17 What is ZooKeeper? Use cases in Hadoop? ZooKeeper, coordination • Distributed coordination service for config, naming, sync
• Maintains configuration information reliably
• Use cases: NameNode HA failover, HBase master election
• Uses Zab protocol for consensus (like Paxos/Raft)
18 What is Sqoop? How does it work? Sqoop, RDBMS • Tool for transferring data between RDBMS and HDFS
• Import: RDBMS → HDFS/Hive (uses MapReduce for parallel transfer)
• Export: HDFS → RDBMS
• Connects via JDBC, splits by primary key for parallelism
19 Sqoop import — incremental modes? Sqoop, incremental • Full import: entire table every time
• Incremental append: only new rows (--incremental append --check-column id)
• Incremental lastmodified: rows modified since last import
• Incremental avoids re-transferring existing data
20 What is Flume? Architecture? Flume, log ingestion • Service for collecting and moving large log/event data
• Sources → Channels → Sinks architecture
• Source: where data comes from (syslog, HTTP, Kafka)
• Channel: buffer (memory or file); Sink: destination (HDFS, HBase)
21 Data locality in Hadoop — why important? Data locality • Process data where it's stored (avoid network transfer)
• YARN schedules tasks on nodes with data blocks
• Three levels: node-local → rack-local → off-rack
• Critical for performance in data-intensive workloads
22 Small files problem in HDFS? Small files • Each file/block needs ~150 bytes metadata in NameNode memory
• Millions of small files → NameNode memory exhaustion
• Solutions: HAR archives, SequenceFiles, CombineFileInputFormat
• Compact small files before storing in HDFS
23 Hadoop Counters — why useful? Counters, debugging • Built-in metrics for tracking MapReduce job progress
• Default: input records, output records, bytes read/written
• Custom counters for application-specific metrics
• Essential for debugging and monitoring job quality
24 DistributedCache in Hadoop? DistributedCache • Mechanism to distribute read-only files to all nodes
• Used for: lookup tables, configuration files, JAR libraries
• Files cached on each node's local filesystem
• Avoids reading from HDFS during each task execution
25 What is Tez? How does it improve Hive? Tez, DAG, Hive • Application framework for building DAG-based processing
• Replaces MapReduce as Hive's execution engine
• DAG model avoids unnecessary intermediate disk writes
• 10x faster than MR for interactive queries
26 Hadoop 2 vs Hadoop 3 improvements? Hadoop 2, Hadoop 3 • Hadoop 3: erasure coding (50% less storage vs 3x replication)
• Support for more than 2 NameNodes (multiple standby)
• GPU support for ML workloads on YARN
• Java 8 minimum, improved shell scripts
27 What is erasure coding in Hadoop 3? Erasure coding • Alternative to replication for fault tolerance
• Uses parity blocks (like RAID) instead of full copies
• 50% storage overhead vs 200% with 3x replication
• Tradeoff: higher CPU for encoding/decoding, suitable for cold data
28 Hadoop HDFS vs cloud storage (S3/ADLS)? HDFS, S3, cloud • HDFS: co-located compute+storage, high throughput, rack-aware
• S3/ADLS: elastic, cheap, durable, separates compute from storage
• Cloud trend: use S3/ADLS as data lake, compute on demand
• HDFS still used in on-prem clusters; cloud prefers object storage
29 What is an InputSplit in MapReduce? InputSplit, mapper • Logical division of input data for a single mapper
• Usually aligned to HDFS block (128 MB)
• Multiple InputSplits = multiple mappers = parallelism
• InputFormat defines how to create InputSplits
30 How to compress data in Hadoop? Codecs? Compression, codec • Snappy: fast, moderate ratio (default for Spark/Parquet)
• LZ4: very fast compression/decompression
• Gzip: best ratio but slow, not splittable
• BZip2: good ratio, splittable, but slow
31 What is a Sequence File? SequenceFile • Binary file format for storing key-value pairs in Hadoop
• Supports compression (record-level or block-level)
• Splittable across MapReduce tasks
• Used to combine many small files into one
32 Explain HDFS SafeMode. SafeMode • Read-only mode during NameNode startup
• NameNode waits until enough DataNodes report blocks
• Ensures minimum replication level before accepting writes
• Exit manually: hdfs dfsadmin -safemode leave
33 What is HDFS snapshot? Snapshot, backup • Read-only, point-in-time copy of a directory
• Created instantly (no data copying — pointer-based)
• Used for backup, recovery, protection against accidental deletion
• Enable: hdfs dfsadmin -allowSnapshot /path
34 HDFS vs HBase — when to use which? HDFS, HBase, compare • HDFS: batch processing, large file storage, sequential reads
• HBase: random read/write, real-time lookups, column-family store
• HDFS for data lakes; HBase for operational workloads
• HBase sits on top of HDFS (uses HDFS for storage)
35 What are Hadoop vendor distributions? Cloudera, Hortonworks • Cloudera (CDP): enterprise Hadoop with management tools
• Hortonworks (merged with Cloudera): open-source focused
• Amazon EMR: managed Hadoop on AWS
• Azure HDInsight: managed Hadoop on Azure

Part 3: Apache Hive¶

Overview¶

Apache Hive is a SQL-based data warehouse built on top of Hadoop. It translates SQL queries (HiveQL) into MapReduce/Tez/Spark jobs for processing data stored in HDFS or cloud storage.

Architecture¶

Source: Apache Hive Wiki — Architecture

Key Concepts¶

Concept Description
Metastore Central schema repository — stores table schemas, partitions, column types (backed by RDBMS like MySQL)
SerDe Serializer/Deserializer — defines how to read/write data formats (JSON, CSV, Avro, ORC)
Internal Table Hive manages both metadata AND data; DROP deletes both
External Table Hive manages only metadata; data lives in external location; DROP keeps data
Partitioning Subdirectories by column values (e.g., /year=2024/month=01/); enables partition pruning
Bucketing Hashes data into fixed number of files by column; improves join and sampling performance
ORC Format Optimized Row Columnar — Hive's preferred format with compression and predicate pushdown
Tez DAG-based execution engine replacing MapReduce (10x faster for Hive queries)

Partitioning vs Bucketing¶

Aspect Partitioning Bucketing
Storage Subdirectories Fixed number of files
Key Column values (date, region) Hash of column
Pruning Partition pruning (skip dirs) Not prunable directly
Performance Great for filter queries Great for joins/sampling
Cardinality Low cardinality columns High cardinality columns
Syntax PARTITIONED BY (col) CLUSTERED BY (col) INTO n BUCKETS

Internal vs External Tables¶

Aspect Internal (Managed) External
Data owned by Hive User / external system
DROP behavior Deletes metadata + data Deletes metadata only
Use case Hive-only data Shared data across tools
Location Default warehouse dir Any HDFS/S3 location
In [4]:
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Hive-style operations using PySpark SQL
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# Create a partitioned table using PySpark (Hive-compatible)
data = [
    ('Alice', 'Sales', 2024, 65000),
    ('Bob',   'Engineering', 2024, 85000),
    ('Carol', 'Sales', 2023, 60000),
    ('Dave',  'Engineering', 2023, 80000),
]
df = spark.createDataFrame(data, ['name', 'dept', 'year', 'salary'])

# Write as partitioned Parquet (emulates Hive partitioned table)
# df.write.partitionBy('year', 'dept').mode('overwrite').parquet('/tmp/hive_demo')

# Register as temp view for SQL queries (similar to Hive)
df.createOrReplaceTempView('employees')

# Hive-style SQL query
spark.sql('''
    SELECT dept, year, AVG(salary) as avg_salary, COUNT(*) as cnt
    FROM employees
    GROUP BY dept, year
    ORDER BY dept, year
''').show()

[Stage 0:>                                                          (0 + 8) / 8]

+-----------+----+----------+---+
|       dept|year|avg_salary|cnt|
+-----------+----+----------+---+
|Engineering|2023|   80000.0|  1|
|Engineering|2024|   85000.0|  1|
|      Sales|2023|   60000.0|  1|
|      Sales|2024|   65000.0|  1|
+-----------+----+----------+---+

Apache Hive — Interview Questions¶

# Question Keywords Answer
1 What is Apache Hive? Hive, SQL • SQL-based data warehouse system on top of Hadoop
• Translates HiveQL to MapReduce/Tez/Spark jobs
• Schema-on-read for data stored in HDFS/S3
• Used for batch analytics, ETL, ad-hoc queries
2 Hive architecture — key components? Architecture, metastore • Client: Beeline, Hive CLI, JDBC/ODBC
• HiveServer2: serves queries to multiple clients
• Metastore: schema registry (backed by RDBMS like MySQL)
• Execution engine: Tez, Spark, or MapReduce
3 What is the Hive Metastore? Metastore, schema • Central repository for Hive table metadata
• Stores: table schemas, partition info, column types, SerDe
• Backed by RDBMS (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Derby)
• Used by Spark, Presto, Trino to read Hive tables
4 Internal (managed) vs external table? Internal, external • Internal: Hive owns data + metadata; DROP deletes both
• External: Hive owns metadata only; DROP keeps data
• External for shared data across multiple tools
• Internal for Hive-only temporary/staging data
5 Partitioning in Hive — why and how? Partition, pruning • Divides table into subdirectories by column values
• Enables partition pruning: skip irrelevant partitions in queries
• Syntax: PARTITIONED BY (year INT, month INT)
• Best for low-cardinality date/region columns
6 Static vs dynamic partitioning? Static, dynamic • Static: manually specify partition values in INSERT
• Dynamic: Hive infers partition values from data
• Dynamic: set hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode=nonstrict
• Dynamic preferred for automated ETL pipelines
7 Bucketing in Hive — when to use? Bucketing, hash • Distributes data into fixed number of files using hash
• Improves join performance (bucketed joins avoid full shuffle)
• Better sampling: read one bucket instead of full table
• Syntax: CLUSTERED BY (col) INTO 32 BUCKETS
8 Partitioning vs bucketing — when each? Partition, bucket, compare • Partitioning: for filter queries (WHERE year=2024)
• Bucketing: for join optimization and sampling
• Combine both: PARTITION BY date + CLUSTER BY user_id
• Avoid over-partitioning (too many small files)
9 What is ORC format? Why Hive prefers it? ORC, columnar • Optimized Row Columnar format — Hive's native format
• Columnar storage with built-in compression (ZLIB, Snappy)
• Supports predicate pushdown and bloom filters
• ACID support for Hive transactions (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE)
10 ORC vs Parquet — which to choose? ORC, Parquet, compare • ORC: optimized for Hive, built-in ACID, bloom filters
• Parquet: Spark ecosystem standard, broader tool support
• ORC better for Hive-heavy environments
• Parquet better for Spark/Presto/multi-tool environments
11 What is a SerDe in Hive? SerDe • Serializer/Deserializer — defines how Hive reads/writes data
• Built-in: LazySimpleSerDe (CSV), JsonSerDe, OrcSerDe
• Custom SerDe for non-standard file formats
• Specified during CREATE TABLE: ROW FORMAT SERDE 'class'
12 What is HiveQL? How different from standard SQL? HiveQL, SQL • Hive Query Language — SQL-like but not fully ANSI SQL
• Supports: SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, window functions, CTAS
• Extensions: LATERAL VIEW, TRANSFORM, DISTRIBUTE BY
• Limitations: limited subquery support, no full UPDATE (until ACID)
13 Execution engines for Hive: MR vs Tez vs Spark? Tez, Spark, execution • MapReduce: original, slow (disk I/O between stages)
• Tez: DAG-based, avoids unnecessary disk writes (10x faster)
• Spark: in-memory execution, fastest for iterative queries
• Tez is default in modern Hive; Spark for mixed workloads
14 Hive ACID transactions — how do they work? ACID, transactions • Hive 3+ supports ACID on ORC tables
• INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE operations
• Uses delta files + compaction (minor/major)
• Requires: ORC format, bucketed tables, transactional=true
15 Compaction in Hive ACID? Minor vs major? Compaction, ACID • Delta files from ACID ops accumulate → slow queries
• Minor compaction: merge delta files together
• Major compaction: merge deltas into base files
• Auto or manual: ALTER TABLE t COMPACT 'major'
16 Views and materialized views in Hive? View, materialized • View: stored query (virtual table, re-executed each time)
• Materialized view: precomputed and stored (faster reads)
• MV auto-refreshed incrementally; used for dashboards
• CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv AS SELECT ...
17 Hive UDF vs UDAF vs UDTF? UDF, UDAF, UDTF • UDF: one row in → one row out (upper(), length())
• UDAF: many rows in → one row out (sum(), count())
• UDTF: one row in → many rows out (explode(), posexplode())
• Custom UDF: extend GenericUDF in Java
18 LATERAL VIEW and explode() in Hive? LATERAL VIEW, explode • explode(): converts array/map to individual rows
• LATERAL VIEW: joins exploded rows back to original table
• Used for: unnesting arrays, parsing JSON arrays
• Example: SELECT * FROM t LATERAL VIEW explode(tags) v AS tag
19 How does Hive handle schema evolution? Schema evolution • Adding columns: ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMNS (safe, backward-compatible)
• Removing columns: not directly supported (mark as deprecated)
• Type changes: limited (widen int→bigint allowed)
• Avro SerDe has best schema evolution support
20 Hive optimization techniques? Optimization, tuning • Partition pruning: query only relevant partitions
• Bucketed joins: avoid shuffle for pre-bucketed tables
• Vectorized execution: process batches of 1024 rows at once
• Cost-based optimizer (CBO): set hive.cbo.enable=true
21 Map-side join in Hive? Map join, broadcast • Small table broadcasted to all mappers (no reduce phase)
• Hint: /*+ MAPJOIN(small_table) */
• Auto: hive.auto.convert.join=true (if table < threshold)
• Much faster than shuffle join for small-large table joins
22 Sort By vs Order By vs Distribute By vs Cluster By? Sort, order, distribute • ORDER BY: global sort (single reducer — slow)
• SORT BY: sort within each reducer (partial sort)
• DISTRIBUTE BY: control how rows go to reducers (by key)
• CLUSTER BY: DISTRIBUTE BY + SORT BY on same column
23 CTAS and INSERT OVERWRITE? CTAS, insert • CTAS: CREATE TABLE new AS SELECT ... (creates + loads)
• INSERT OVERWRITE: replaces data in existing table/partition
• INSERT INTO: appends data
• CTAS great for creating derived/summary tables
24 Window functions in Hive? Window, rank • ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), DENSE_RANK()
• SUM/AVG/COUNT OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)
• LAG(), LEAD(): access previous/next row values
• Used for: running totals, deduplication, ranking
25 How to handle skewed data in Hive? Skew, optimization • SKEWED BY: marks column with known skewed values
• Splits skewed keys into separate files
• List bucketing: directory per skewed value
• Also: increase reducers, use MAPJOIN for skewed joins
26 Hive metastore modes? Remote vs embedded? Metastore, remote • Embedded: runs in-process with Hive client (single-user, testing)
• Local: separate process, same machine
• Remote: standalone service (recommended for production)
• Remote enables multiple clients (Spark, Presto) to share
27 Vectorized execution in Hive? Vectorization • Processes batches of 1024 rows at once instead of row-by-row
• Reduces function calls and CPU cache misses
• Enable: set hive.vectorized.execution.enabled=true
• Only supported with ORC format
28 Cost-Based Optimizer (CBO) in Hive? CBO, optimizer • Uses column-level statistics to choose optimal query plans
• Computes: join order, join strategy, parallelism
• Enable: set hive.cbo.enable=true
• Requires: ANALYZE TABLE t COMPUTE STATISTICS FOR COLUMNS
29 Hive with Spark engine — how is it configured? Hive, Spark • Set hive.execution.engine=spark in hive-site.xml
• Requires Spark on the cluster + compatible Hive version
• Benefits: in-memory processing, faster than Tez for iterative
• Hive-on-Spark is different from SparkSQL (different query engines)
30 What is HCatalog? HCatalog • Table and storage management layer for Hadoop
• Abstracts Hive metastore as shared schema registry
• Allows Pig, MapReduce, Spark to read Hive tables
• Part of Apache Hive project
31 Hive vs Spark SQL? Hive, SparkSQL, compare • Hive: batch-oriented, disk-based, good for large ETL
• Spark SQL: in-memory, faster, interactive queries
• Hive: mature metastore integration, ACID on ORC
• Spark SQL: preferred for modern analytics
32 How to load data into Hive? Load data, Hive • LOAD DATA: moves/copies data from HDFS/local to table
• INSERT INTO: result of a query into a table
• CTAS: create table from SELECT
• External: just point LOCATION to existing data
33 Hive file formats — when to use each? Format, ORC, Parquet • Text: simple, human-readable, no compression — testing only
• ORC: Hive default, ACID, bloom filters, best for Hive queries
• Parquet: Spark default, cross-platform, broader tool support
• Avro: streaming, schema evolution, Kafka + Hive integration
34 Hive indexes — do they exist? Index, Hive • Hive 2.x had indexes but DEPRECATED in Hive 3+
• Replaced by: ORC built-in indexes, bloom filters, data skipping
• Materialized views serve similar purpose
• ZORDER (in Delta/Iceberg) replaces traditional indexing
35 Hive on cloud — alternatives? Hive, cloud • AWS Athena: serverless SQL on S3 (Presto-based, not Hive)
• Azure HDInsight with Hive
• Databricks SQL replaces Hive for lakehouse analytics
• Google BigQuery: serverless warehouse

Part 4: Apache HBase¶

Overview¶

Apache HBase is a NoSQL, column-family, wide-column store built on top of HDFS. It provides random, real-time read/write access to Big Data — filling the gap HDFS has (batch-only, no random access).

Data Model¶

Source: TutorialsPoint — HBase Architecture

Key Points: Each row key maps to column families; columns within a family are stored together; cells can be empty (sparse storage).

Architecture¶

Component Role
HMaster Cluster coordinator — assigns regions, handles DDL, load balancing
RegionServer Worker — serves reads/writes for assigned regions
Region Subset of a table's rows (contiguous range of row keys)
WAL (Write-Ahead Log) Durability — logs writes before applying to MemStore
MemStore In-memory write buffer per column family
HFile On-disk sorted file (stored in HDFS)
ZooKeeper Cluster coordination, RegionServer health, master election

Read/Write Path¶

WRITE: Client → RegionServer → WAL (durability) → MemStore (memory) → MemStore flush → HFile (disk/HDFS)

READ: Client → BlockCache (if cached) → MemStore → HFile

Bloom filters speed up HFile lookups

Compaction¶

Type Description
Minor Merges several small HFiles into fewer larger ones (fast, no deletions)
Major Merges ALL HFiles for a region into one, applies deletions and TTL (expensive)

Apache HBase — Interview Questions¶

# Question Keywords Answer
1 What is HBase? When to use it? HBase, NoSQL • Column-family NoSQL database on top of HDFS
• Real-time random read/write access to Big Data
• Use when: millions of rows, fast lookups by key, sparse data
• Not suitable for: complex queries, joins, analytics (use Hive/Spark)
2 HBase data model — row key, column family, qualifier? Data model • Row Key: unique primary key, sorted lexicographically
• Column Family: group of columns stored together (defined at table creation)
• Column Qualifier: specific column within a family (dynamic, added at write time)
• Cell: row_key + cf + qualifier + timestamp → value
3 HBase architecture — HMaster vs RegionServer? Architecture • HMaster: coordinator — DDL, region assignment, load balancing
• RegionServer: worker — handles reads/writes for assigned regions
• Region: contiguous range of rows (auto-splits when too large)
• ZooKeeper: health monitoring, master election
4 Write path in HBase? Write, WAL, MemStore • Write → WAL (Write-Ahead Log for durability)
• Write → MemStore (in-memory buffer per column family)
• When MemStore fills → flush to HFile on HDFS
• ACK sent to client after WAL + MemStore writes
5 Read path in HBase? Read, BlockCache • Check BlockCache (LRU cache for recently read blocks)
• Check MemStore (recent unflushed writes)
• Check HFiles on disk (use bloom filters to skip irrelevant files)
• Merge results from all sources for final response
6 What is the WAL (Write-Ahead Log)? WAL, durability • Append-only log that records every write operation
• Ensures durability: if RegionServer crashes, replay WAL
• Written BEFORE MemStore for guaranteed persistence
• Can be disabled for speed (at risk of data loss)
7 MemStore and HFile — relationship? MemStore, HFile • MemStore: in-memory sorted buffer for writes
• HFile: immutable, sorted on-disk file in HDFS
• MemStore flushes to HFile when size threshold reached
• Multiple HFiles per region → compaction merges them
8 Minor vs major compaction? Compaction, minor, major • Minor: merges small HFiles into fewer larger ones (fast)
• Major: merges ALL HFiles into one, removes deleted/expired data
• Minor runs automatically; major is scheduled or manual
• Major is expensive — schedule during low traffic
9 Region splitting — how and why? Region, split • Region grows → auto-splits into two at midpoint of row keys
• Increases parallelism (more regions → more RegionServers)
• Split threshold configurable (default ~10 GB)
• Pre-splitting recommended for even distribution at table creation
10 Row key design best practices? Row key, design • Keep row keys short (reduces storage and index size)
• Avoid sequential keys (causes hotspotting on one region)
• Use salting/hashing to distribute writes evenly
• Design for most common query patterns (prefix scans)
11 What is hotspotting? How to prevent it? Hotspot, skew • All reads/writes going to one RegionServer (uneven load)
• Caused by sequential/monotonic row keys (timestamps, IDs)
• Solutions: salting (random prefix), hashing, reverse timestamps
• Pre-split table with well-distributed split points
12 HBase vs Cassandra? HBase, Cassandra, compare • HBase: CP (strong consistency), master-slave, runs on HDFS
• Cassandra: AP (eventual consistency), peer-to-peer, own storage
• HBase for: Hadoop ecosystem, strong consistency needs
• Cassandra for: global distribution, high write throughput
13 HBase vs HDFS — when to use which? HBase, HDFS • HDFS: batch processing, large sequential reads, append-only
• HBase: random real-time read/write on key-value data
• HDFS for data lakes; HBase for operational lookups
• HBase stores data ON HDFS but provides random access layer
14 What are bloom filters in HBase? Bloom filter • Probabilistic data structure to check if key exists in HFile
• Skip reading HFiles that don't contain requested row
• Reduces disk I/O significantly for point lookups
• Types: ROW (check row key) or ROWCOL (row + column)
15 Block cache in HBase? BlockCache, LRU • LRU cache storing recently read HFile blocks in memory
• Speeds up repeated reads (avoids disk I/O)
• Two types: on-heap (LRU) and off-heap (BucketCache)
• Configurable per column family
16 What is Apache Phoenix? Phoenix, SQL on HBase • SQL layer on top of HBase (JDBC interface)
• Translates SQL queries to HBase scans/gets
• Supports: secondary indexes, joins, aggregations
• Makes HBase accessible to BI tools and SQL users
17 HBase schema design principles? Schema, column family • Minimize column families (1-3 max; each has its own MemStore/HFile)
• Group frequently accessed columns in same family
• Wide rows (many columns) preferred over tall rows (many rows)
• Denormalize: avoid joins (not supported in HBase)
18 How does HBase achieve fault tolerance? Fault tolerance • WAL ensures writes survive RegionServer crashes
• Data stored in HDFS (replicated across DataNodes)
• ZooKeeper detects failed RegionServers
• HMaster reassigns regions from failed server to healthy ones
19 TTL (Time-To-Live) in HBase? TTL, expiry • Auto-delete cells older than TTL duration
• Set per column family: alter 't', {NAME=>'cf', TTL=>'86400'}
• Expired data removed during major compaction
• Useful for: session data, logs, temporary caches
20 Versioning in HBase? Versioning, timestamp • Each cell stores multiple versions (by timestamp)
• Default: 1 version kept (configurable per CF: VERSIONS => 3)
• Query specific version: get.setTimeStamp(ts)
• Older versions removed during compaction
21 Coprocessors in HBase? Coprocessor • Server-side code execution on RegionServers (like stored procedures)
• Observer: hooks before/after operations (triggers)
• Endpoint: custom RPC calls for server-side aggregations
• Used for: secondary indexing, access control, aggregations
22 HBase namespace? Namespace • Logical grouping of tables (like databases in RDBMS)
• Default namespaces: 'default' and 'hbase' (system)
• Allows: quota management, resource isolation per namespace
• Syntax: create_namespace 'my_ns' → create 'my_ns:table1', 'cf'
23 Scan vs Get in HBase? Scan, Get • Get: retrieve single row by exact row key (fast, O(1))
• Scan: range scan over multiple rows (slower, sequential)
• Scan with start/stop row for efficient range queries
• Filters: SingleColumnValueFilter, PrefixFilter to narrow scans
24 HBase replication? Replication • Asynchronous replication between HBase clusters
• WAL-based: replays WAL entries from source to sink cluster
• Master-slave or master-master topologies
• Used for: disaster recovery, geographic distribution
25 HBase on cloud — alternatives? Cloud, HBase • AWS: EMR with HBase, DynamoDB (managed NoSQL)
• Azure: HDInsight with HBase, Cosmos DB
• GCP: Bigtable (managed HBase-compatible, same API)
• Cloud Bigtable is the most popular HBase cloud alternative

Part 5: Apache Cassandra¶

Overview¶

Apache Cassandra is a distributed, peer-to-peer, wide-column NoSQL database designed for high availability and massive write throughput. It sacrifices strong consistency for availability (AP in CAP theorem).

Architecture — Peer-to-Peer (No Master)¶

Source: Apache Cassandra Official

Data Model¶

Concept Description
Keyspace Top-level namespace (like database in RDBMS), defines replication strategy
Table Collection of rows, defined by CREATE TABLE
Partition Key Determines which node stores the data (hashed by partitioner)
Clustering Key Determines sort order within a partition
Primary Key = Partition Key + Clustering Key(s)
Column Name-value pair within a row

Consistency Levels¶

Level Meaning
ONE Only 1 replica must respond (fastest, least consistent)
QUORUM Majority of replicas must respond (balances consistency + speed)
ALL All replicas must respond (strongest consistency, highest latency)
LOCAL_QUORUM Quorum within local data center (multi-DC deployments)

Write Path¶

WRITE: Client → Coordinator Node → Commit Log (durability) → MemTable (memory) → MemTable flush → SSTable (immutable sorted file on disk)

SSTables compacted periodically (merge + remove tombstones)

Read Path¶

READ: Client → Coordinator → Check MemTable → Check SSTables

  • Bloom filter: skip SSTables that don't have the key
  • Partition index + compression offsets → locate data
  • Merge results from MemTable + SSTables → return

Apache Cassandra — Interview Questions¶

# Question Keywords Answer
1 What is Cassandra? Key features? Cassandra, NoSQL • Distributed peer-to-peer NoSQL database
• Designed for high write throughput and availability
• AP in CAP theorem (eventually consistent)
• Linear scalability: add more nodes = more capacity
2 Cassandra architecture — how is it different from HBase? Architecture, peer-to-peer • No master node — all nodes are equal (peer-to-peer)
• Uses gossip protocol for node discovery
• Data distributed via consistent hashing (token ring)
• HBase has master (HMaster); Cassandra has no SPOF
3 What is a partition key? Why critical? Partition key, design • Part of primary key that determines data placement
• Hashed by partitioner to assign data to a node
• Queries MUST include partition key (or full table scan)
• Poor partition key = data skew = hot nodes
4 Partition key vs clustering key? Primary key, clustering • Partition key: which node stores the data (hash-distributed)
• Clustering key: sort order within the partition
• Primary key = (partition_key, clustering_key)
• Example: PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), created_at)
5 What is a keyspace? Keyspace, replication • Top-level container (like a database in RDBMS)
• Defines replication strategy and factor
• SimpleStrategy: single DC; NetworkTopologyStrategy: multi-DC
• CREATE KEYSPACE ks WITH replication = {'class': 'NetworkTopologyStrategy', 'dc1': 3}
6 Consistency levels in Cassandra? Consistency, quorum • ONE: fastest, single replica (risk of stale reads)
• QUORUM: majority (RF/2 + 1) — balanced
• ALL: strongest but slowest (all replicas must respond)
• LOCAL_QUORUM: quorum within local data center
7 How does Cassandra achieve high availability? Availability, replication • Peer-to-peer: no single point of failure
• Data replicated across multiple nodes (replication factor)
• Hinted handoff: missed writes stored and delivered later
• Multi-datacenter replication for geographic redundancy
8 Write path in Cassandra? Write, commit log • Write → Commit Log (append-only, durability)
• Write → MemTable (in-memory sorted structure)
• MemTable full → flush to SSTable (immutable, on disk)
• ACK after commit log + memtable (fast writes)
9 Read path in Cassandra? Read, SSTable • Check MemTable for recent unflushed data
• Check SSTables with bloom filter (skip irrelevant ones)
• Use partition index + compression offset to locate data
• Merge results from multiple sources → return to client
10 What are SSTables? Why immutable? SSTable, immutable • Sorted String Tables — immutable on-disk data files
• Immutability enables: fast sequential writes, no locks
• Old data cleaned up via compaction (merge + tombstone removal)
• Each SSTable has: data file, index file, bloom filter
11 Compaction strategies in Cassandra? Compaction, strategy • STCS (Size-Tiered): merge similarly-sized SSTables (write-optimized)
• LCS (Leveled): level-based merging (read-optimized, less space amplification)
• TWCS (Time-Window): for time-series data (compact within time windows)
• Choose based on workload: write-heavy → STCS, read-heavy → LCS
12 What are tombstones? Why are they a problem? Tombstone, delete • Marker indicating deleted data (not physically removed immediately)
• Prevents deleted data from reappearing via replication
• Problem: too many tombstones slow down reads (must scan them)
• Removed during compaction after gc_grace_seconds (default 10 days)
13 Gossip protocol in Cassandra? Gossip, protocol • Peer-to-peer communication protocol for node discovery
• Every second, each node shares state with 1-3 random nodes
• Propagates: node status (alive/dead), token ownership, schema
• Eventually all nodes learn about entire cluster state
14 What is a snitch in Cassandra? Snitch, topology • Determines network topology (which DC and rack a node belongs to)
• Used for: replica placement, routing queries to nearest node
• Types: SimpleSnitch, GossipingPropertyFileSnitch, RackInferringSnitch
• GossipingPropertyFileSnitch recommended for production
15 Lightweight transactions (LWT) in Cassandra? LWT, Paxos • IF NOT EXISTS / IF conditions for conditional writes
• Uses Paxos consensus protocol (4 round trips — slow)
• Provides linearizable consistency for specific operations
• Use sparingly — significant performance overhead
16 Data modeling best practices in Cassandra? Modeling, denormalize • Design tables around query patterns (not relationships)
• Denormalize: duplicate data across tables for different access patterns
• One table per query pattern (no joins in Cassandra)
• Avoid large partitions (>100MB causes GC pressure)
17 Anti-patterns in Cassandra data modeling? Anti-pattern • Using Cassandra like an RDBMS (normalizing, expecting joins)
• Large partitions (unbounded growth on partition key)
• Too many tombstones from frequent deletes
• ALLOW FILTERING in production (full table scan)
18 What is hinted handoff? Hinted handoff • When a destination node is down, coordinator stores the write as a hint
• Once node comes back, hints are delivered (eventual consistency)
• Timeout: hints expire after 3 hours by default
• Ensures writes aren't lost during temporary failures
19 Read repair in Cassandra? Read repair • During reads, coordinator compares responses from replicas
• If replicas have different versions, latest version sent to stale replicas
• Ensures eventual consistency across replicas
• Background read repair runs on a percentage of reads
20 Anti-entropy repair (nodetool repair)? Repair, anti-entropy • Full repair: compares all data across replicas using Merkle trees
• Fixes inconsistencies that hinted handoff and read repair missed
• Must run within gc_grace_seconds to prevent zombie data
• Schedule: weekly or based on tombstone pressure
21 Secondary indexes in Cassandra — when to use? Secondary index • Allows querying on non-partition-key columns
• Implementation: local index per node (not global)
• Good for: low-cardinality columns, queries on single partition
• Bad for: high-cardinality columns (scatter-gather across all nodes)
22 Materialized views in Cassandra? Materialized view • Server-maintained copy of base table with different primary key
• Auto-updated when base table changes
• Enables querying by different access patterns
• Overhead: extra storage, write amplification, consistency lag
23 Cassandra vs MongoDB? Cassandra, MongoDB, compare • Cassandra: wide-column, linear scalability, AP, peer-to-peer
• MongoDB: document store, rich queries, CP (with replica sets)
• Cassandra: better for writes, time-series, massive scale
• MongoDB: better for flexible schema, aggregation framework
24 Multi-datacenter replication in Cassandra? Multi-DC, replication • NetworkTopologyStrategy: define replication factor per DC
• Data automatically replicated to nodes in remote DCs
• LOCAL_QUORUM: read/write within local DC only
• Enables: disaster recovery, low-latency global access
25 What is ALLOW FILTERING? Why avoid it? ALLOW FILTERING • Enables queries without partition key (full cluster scan)
• Extremely slow and expensive on large datasets
• Only use for: small data, development/debugging
• Production: always query by partition key
26 Tunable consistency — what does it mean? Tunable, consistency • Cassandra allows PER-QUERY consistency level
• Trade consistency for speed or vice versa per operation
• Strong read: write at QUORUM + read at QUORUM (R+W > N)
• Fast write: write at ONE, read at ONE (eventual)
27 What is a coordinator node in Cassandra? Coordinator • The node that receives the client request
• Routes request to the correct replica nodes
• Aggregates responses based on consistency level
• Any node can be a coordinator (peer-to-peer)
28 How to handle time-series data in Cassandra? Time-series • Partition by entity (sensor_id, device_id)
• Cluster by timestamp (descending for latest-first)
• Use TWCS compaction strategy
• Set TTL for automatic data expiry
29 Cassandra on cloud — managed services? Cloud, Cassandra • DataStax Astra: fully managed Cassandra-as-a-Service
• AWS Keyspaces: Cassandra-compatible managed service
• Azure Cosmos DB: Cassandra API compatibility
• Managed services reduce operational overhead
30 CQL (Cassandra Query Language) — how different from SQL? CQL, SQL • CQL looks like SQL but with restrictions
• No JOINs, no subqueries, limited aggregations
• Must always query by partition key
• No ALTER to change primary key after creation

Part 6: Apache Spark — Core Concepts¶

What is Apache Spark?¶

Apache Spark is a distributed data processing engine designed for large-scale analytics and ML. Unlike MapReduce (disk-based), Spark performs in-memory computation using a DAG execution model, making it 10-100x faster for iterative and interactive workloads.

Spark Architecture¶

Source: Apache Spark Official Documentation

Component Roles¶
Component Role Key Details
Driver Brain — creates DAG, schedules tasks Runs main(), creates SparkSession, collects results
Executor Muscle — runs tasks, stores data JVM process on worker node, reports to driver
Cluster Manager Resource allocator YARN, Mesos, Kubernetes, Standalone
SparkSession Unified entry point Replaces SQLContext + HiveContext + SparkContext
SparkContext Low-level RDD entry point Accessible as spark.sparkContext

Spark APIs (RDD → DataFrame → Dataset)¶

Feature RDD DataFrame Dataset (Scala/Java)
Abstraction Low-level objects Named columns (table) Typed objects + table
Schema No schema Schema-aware Schema + type-safe
Optimization None (manual) Catalyst + Tungsten Catalyst + Tungsten
Language Scala, Java, Python All Scala, Java only
Performance Slowest Fast (optimized) Fast + type-safe
Best for Custom logic, unstructured 90% of workloads Type-safe structured

DAG — Directed Acyclic Graph¶

When an action is triggered (e.g., count(), collect()), Spark builds a DAG of transformations and breaks it into stages and tasks:

Transformations (lazy) → Action (eager) triggers DAG execution:

read → filter → map → groupBy → count

(narrow transforms)       (wide = shuffle)

  • Stage boundary = shuffle (wide transformation)
  • Each stage → N tasks (one per partition)
  • Tasks sent to executors for parallel execution

Narrow vs Wide Transformations¶

Type Data Movement Stage Boundary Examples
Narrow No shuffle — each partition → one partition No map, filter, flatMap, withColumn, select
Wide Shuffle — data redistributed across partitions Yes groupBy, reduceByKey, join, distinct, repartition

Lazy Evaluation¶

Spark defers execution of transformations until an action is called:

  • Allows Catalyst to optimize the entire plan before execution
  • Avoids unnecessary computations
  • Transformations: build the plan (lazy)
  • Actions: trigger execution (eager)
Transformations (Lazy) Actions (Eager)
select, filter, map, join count, collect, show, write
withColumn, groupBy, agg first, take, reduce, foreach
union, distinct, cache saveAsTable, toPandas

Catalyst Optimizer + Tungsten Engine¶

Source: Databricks — Catalyst Optimizer

Catalyst = decides WHAT & HOW (query planning) — Brain of Spark SQL

Tungsten = executes FAST (off-heap memory, WSCG, cache-aware) — Muscle

Catalyst Optimizations¶
  • Predicate pushdown: push filters closer to data source
  • Column pruning: read only needed columns
  • Constant folding: evaluate constant expressions at compile time
  • Join reordering: optimize join order based on statistics
Tungsten Optimizations¶
  • Off-heap memory: bypasses JVM garbage collection
  • Whole-Stage Code Generation (WSCG): compiles query stages into optimized JVM bytecode
  • Cache-aware computation: organizes data for CPU cache efficiency
  • Binary processing: operates on binary data directly, avoiding serialization overhead

Spark Memory Management¶

Spark Executor JVM Heap
Reserved Memory (300 MB fixed)
User Memory (~40%) — UDFs, user data structures
Spark Memory (Unified) — (~60%)
Execution Memory
Shuffles, joins, sorts, aggregations		 Storage Memory
Cached RDDs, broadcast variables
Off-Heap Memory (optional, outside JVM GC)

Execution and Storage memory can dynamically borrow from each other (Unified Memory Model, Spark 1.6+)

Dynamic boundary: Execution can borrow from Storage (evicts cached data) and vice versa.

Config Default Purpose
spark.memory.fraction 0.6 Fraction of heap for unified memory
spark.memory.storageFraction 0.5 Initial division between storage and execution
spark.executor.memory 1g Total executor heap size
spark.executor.memoryOverhead 10% Off-heap memory for JVM overhead

Cache vs Persist¶

Method Description
df.cache() Shortcut for persist(MEMORY_ONLY)
df.persist(level) Choose storage level (MEMORY_ONLY, MEMORY_AND_DISK, etc.)
df.unpersist() Remove from cache

Storage Levels:

  • MEMORY_ONLY — fastest, loses data if not enough memory
  • MEMORY_AND_DISK — spills to disk if memory runs out
  • DISK_ONLY — only on disk (slow but safe)
  • MEMORY_ONLY_2 — with 2x replication (fault-tolerant)

Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) — Spark 3.0+¶

AQE dynamically optimizes queries at runtime based on actual statistics:

Feature Description
Dynamic join strategy Switches sort-merge to broadcast if input is smaller than expected
Skew join handling Splits skewed partitions into smaller tasks
Partition coalescing Reduces empty/small shuffle partitions
Enable spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true (default in Spark 3.2+)

Deployment Modes¶

Mode Driver Location Use Case
Client On submitting machine Interactive, debugging
Cluster On cluster node Production, scheduled jobs
Local Single JVM (local[*]) Development, testing
In [5]:
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Spark Core — exploring the execution model
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# 1. RDD basics
rdd = sc.parallelize([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], 4)  # 4 partitions
print(f'Partitions: {rdd.getNumPartitions()}')
print(f'Sum: {rdd.reduce(lambda a, b: a + b)}')

# 2. Transformations vs Actions
# Transformations are LAZY (build DAG)
filtered = rdd.filter(lambda x: x > 3)      # lazy
mapped = filtered.map(lambda x: x * 10)      # lazy
# Action triggers execution
print(f'Result: {mapped.collect()}')           # [40, 50, 60, 70, 80]

# 3. View execution plan
df = spark.range(1000)
result = df.filter('id > 500').groupBy((F.col('id') % 10).alias('bucket')).count()
result.explain(True)  # Shows Catalyst optimization plan

Partitions: 4
Sum: 36
Result: [40, 50, 60, 70, 80]
== Parsed Logical Plan ==
'Aggregate ['`%`('id, 10) AS bucket#33], ['`%`('id, 10) AS bucket#33, 'count(1) AS count#34]
+- Filter (id#29L > cast(500 as bigint))
   +- Range (0, 1000, step=1, splits=Some(8))

== Analyzed Logical Plan ==
bucket: bigint, count: bigint
Aggregate [(id#29L % cast(10 as bigint))], [(id#29L % cast(10 as bigint)) AS bucket#33L, count(1) AS count#34L]
+- Filter (id#29L > cast(500 as bigint))
   +- Range (0, 1000, step=1, splits=Some(8))

== Optimized Logical Plan ==
Aggregate [_groupingexpression#37L], [_groupingexpression#37L AS bucket#33L, count(1) AS count#34L]
+- Project [(id#29L % 10) AS _groupingexpression#37L]
   +- Filter (id#29L > 500)
      +- Range (0, 1000, step=1, splits=Some(8))

== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[_groupingexpression#37L], functions=[count(1)], output=[bucket#33L, count#34L])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(_groupingexpression#37L, 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS, [plan_id=77]
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[_groupingexpression#37L], functions=[partial_count(1)], output=[_groupingexpression#37L, count#39L])
         +- Project [(id#29L % 10) AS _groupingexpression#37L]
            +- Filter (id#29L > 500)
               +- Range (0, 1000, step=1, splits=8)
In [6]:
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Accumulators and Broadcast Variables
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# Accumulator — aggregation variable shared across tasks
error_count = sc.accumulator(0)

def process_row(x):
    global error_count
    if x < 0:
        error_count.add(1)
    return abs(x)

data = sc.parallelize([1, -2, 3, -4, 5])
result = data.map(process_row).collect()
print(f'Processed: {result}')
print(f'Errors found: {error_count.value}')  # 2

# Broadcast Variable — read-only variable sent once to all executors
lookup = {'A': 'Alice', 'B': 'Bob', 'C': 'Carol'}
broadcast_lookup = sc.broadcast(lookup)

codes = sc.parallelize(['A', 'B', 'C', 'A'])
names = codes.map(lambda c: broadcast_lookup.value.get(c, 'Unknown'))
print(f'Names: {names.collect()}')  # ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carol', 'Alice']

Processed: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Errors found: 2
Names: ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carol', 'Alice']

Apache Spark Core — Interview Questions (Part 1)¶

# Question Keywords Answer
1 What is Apache Spark? Why faster than MapReduce? Spark, speed • Distributed data processing engine for analytics and ML
• In-memory computation (avoids disk I/O between stages)
• DAG execution model (optimizes pipeline vs rigid Map→Reduce)
• Supports multiple APIs: RDD, DataFrame, SQL, Streaming, MLlib
2 What is PySpark? How does Python interact with Spark? PySpark, Py4J • Python API for Apache Spark
• Uses Py4J bridge library for Python→JVM communication
• Python commands translated to JVM calls, executed on cluster
• Best of Python ecosystem + Spark's distributed power
3 SparkSession vs SparkContext? SparkSession, SparkContext • SparkSession: unified entry point (Spark 2.0+) for DataFrame/SQL/Streaming
• SparkContext: low-level entry point for RDD API
• SparkSession wraps SparkContext internally
• Always use SparkSession; access SC via spark.sparkContext
4 What is an RDD? Key features? RDD, resilient • Resilient Distributed Dataset — immutable, partitioned collection
• Resilient: fault-tolerant via lineage (recompute lost partitions)
• Distributed: data split across cluster nodes
• Immutable: transformations create new RDDs, never modify
5 DataFrame vs RDD — when each? DataFrame, RDD, compare • DataFrame: structured, schema-aware, Catalyst-optimized
• RDD: unstructured, fine-grained control, no optimization
• DataFrame is 2-10x faster due to Catalyst + Tungsten
• Use RDD only for: custom algorithms, unstructured data
6 RDD vs DataFrame vs Dataset — comparison? RDD, DataFrame, Dataset • RDD: no schema, manual optimization, all languages
• DataFrame: schema-aware, Catalyst optimized, all languages
• Dataset: schema + type-safe, Catalyst optimized, Scala/Java only
• PySpark: DataFrame recommended (Dataset not available)
7 Transformation vs action in Spark? Transformation, action • Transformation: returns new RDD/DataFrame (lazy — map, filter, join)
• Action: triggers computation, returns value (eager — count, collect, show)
• Lazy eval builds DAG; action triggers entire execution
• One action can trigger execution of many transformations
8 What is lazy evaluation? Why important? Lazy, evaluation • Spark defers execution of transformations until an action is called
• Builds a DAG of operations, then optimizes entire plan
• Enables: predicate pushdown, pipeline optimization
• Avoids unnecessary computation (only computes what's needed)
9 Explain the DAG in Spark. DAG, execution • Directed Acyclic Graph — sequence of transformations on data
• Nodes = operations, edges = dependencies
• DAG broken into stages at shuffle boundaries
• Stages broken into tasks (one per partition)
10 How does the DAG Scheduler work? DAG Scheduler, stages • Triggered when an action is called
• Divides DAG into stages (at wide transformation boundaries)
• Within each stage, narrow transformations are pipelined
• Submits stages to Task Scheduler → dispatches tasks to executors
11 Narrow vs wide transformations — examples? Narrow, wide • Narrow: each partition → one output partition (no shuffle)
Examples: map, filter, flatMap, withColumn, select
• Wide: requires shuffle across partitions (stage boundary)
Examples: groupBy, reduceByKey, join, distinct, repartition
12 What is a shuffle? Why expensive? Shuffle, cost • Redistribution of data across partitions (wide transformation)
• Involves: serialization, disk I/O, network transfer, deserialization
• Most expensive operation in Spark
• Minimize: use broadcast joins, pre-partition data, tune shuffle partitions
13 What is a Spark Executor? Executor, worker • Worker process (JVM) running on cluster nodes
• Executes tasks assigned by the driver
• Stores data in memory/disk (cache, shuffle)
• Reports status back to driver; reschedule if failed
14 What is the Spark Driver? Driver, coordinator • Central coordinator of Spark application
• Runs main program, creates SparkSession
• Builds DAG, optimizes via Catalyst, schedules tasks
• Collects results from executors
15 Cluster managers supported by Spark? Cluster manager • Standalone: Spark's built-in, simple, easy setup
• YARN: Hadoop ecosystem, multi-tenant, production standard
• Mesos: general-purpose cluster manager
• Kubernetes: modern containerized, elastic scaling
16 What is the Catalyst Optimizer? Catalyst, optimizer • Spark SQL's query optimization framework
• Phases: Analysis → Logical Optimization → Physical Planning → Code Generation
• Rule-based + cost-based optimization
• Enables DataFrame/SQL performance comparable to hand-tuned code
17 What is the Tungsten Engine? Tungsten, engine • Spark's execution engine for CPU and memory optimization
• Whole-Stage Code Generation: compiles queries to JVM bytecode
• Off-heap memory management: bypasses JVM GC
• Cache-aware computation: organizes data for CPU efficiency
18 Catalyst vs Tungsten — difference? Catalyst, Tungsten • Catalyst = brain — decides WHAT and HOW (query plan)
• Tungsten = muscle — executes FAST (memory, CPU optimization)
• Catalyst: predicate pushdown, join reordering, pruning
• Tungsten: codegen, off-heap, binary processing
19 What is partitioning? Why important? Partitioning • How Spark splits data across executors for parallel processing
• Each partition processed by one task on one core
• Too few partitions: under-utilization
• Too many partitions: scheduling overhead. Rule: 2-4x number of cores
20 Cache vs persist? Storage levels? Cache, persist • cache() = persist(MEMORY_ONLY) — shortcut
• persist(level) — choose: MEMORY_ONLY, MEMORY_AND_DISK, DISK_ONLY
• MEMORY_ONLY_2, MEMORY_AND_DISK_2: with replication
• unpersist() to remove from cache
21 What is broadcast join? When to use? Broadcast, join • Small table broadcasted to all executors (avoids shuffle)
• Used when one side is small enough for memory
• Hint: broadcast(small_df) or config threshold
• Much faster than shuffle-based sort-merge join
22 What are accumulators? Accumulator, counter • Write-only shared variables for aggregation across tasks
• Used for: counters, sums, monitoring/debugging
• Read-only from driver, write-only from executors
• May double-count on task retries — use for monitoring, not core logic
23 What are broadcast variables? Broadcast, variable • Read-only data distributed once to all executors
• Avoids sending copy with every task (reduces network)
• Immutable; stored in executor memory for reuse
• Common use: lookup tables, config, map-side joins
24 What is lineage? How does it enable fault tolerance? Lineage, fault tolerance • Record of all transformations applied to derive an RDD/DataFrame
• If partition is lost → Spark recomputes from lineage (DAG)
• No data replication needed (unlike HBase/HDFS replication)
• Lineage can grow → use checkpointing to truncate
25 What is checkpointing in Spark? Checkpoint • Saving RDD/DataFrame state to durable storage (HDFS/S3)
• Truncates lineage — avoids expensive recomputation of long chains
• Required in Structured Streaming for fault recovery
• Two types: reliable (to HDFS) and local (for testing)

Apache Spark Core — Interview Questions (Part 2)¶

# Question Keywords Answer
26 Explain Spark's in-memory computation model. In-memory • Keeps intermediate results in executor memory (not disk)
• Cache/persist DataFrames for reuse across actions
• Tungsten uses off-heap for efficient memory layout
• Spills to disk when memory is insufficient
27 Coalesce vs repartition? Coalesce, repartition • coalesce(n): reduce partitions WITHOUT full shuffle (faster)
• repartition(n): increase/decrease WITH full shuffle (even distribution)
• coalesce for: writing fewer output files, post-join reduction
• repartition for: increasing parallelism, pre-join distribution
28 What is data skew? How to handle it? Skew, salting • Uneven data distribution — one partition much larger than others
• Causes: hot keys in groupBy/join → straggler tasks
• Solutions: salting (random prefix to keys), broadcast join, AQE
• AQE (Spark 3): auto-splits skewed partitions at runtime
29 What is AQE (Adaptive Query Execution)? AQE, adaptive • Runtime query optimization in Spark 3.0+
• Dynamic join strategy: converts shuffle→broadcast mid-execution
• Skew join handling: splits skewed partitions automatically
• Partition coalescing: merges empty/small shuffle partitions
30 What is speculative execution? Speculative • Launches duplicate of slow tasks on other executors
• First to finish wins; other is killed
• Handles: hardware degradation, data skew
• Enable: spark.speculation=true
31 Dynamic allocation in Spark? Dynamic, allocation • Auto-scales executors up/down based on workload
• Scale up: when pending tasks exist
• Scale down: idle executors released after timeout
• Requires external shuffle service for safe executor removal
32 Execution vs storage memory in Spark? Memory, management • Unified memory region shared between execution and storage
• Execution: shuffles, joins, sorts, aggregations
• Storage: cached DataFrames, broadcast variables
• Can borrow from each other; execution can evict storage
33 Spark deployment modes — client vs cluster? Client, cluster • Client mode: driver on submitting machine (interactive use)
• Cluster mode: driver on cluster node (production jobs)
• Local mode: everything on one JVM (development/testing)
• Use cluster mode for scheduled production pipelines
34 How to optimize joins in Spark? Join, optimize • Broadcast join for small-large table pairs
• Repartition both sides on join key before joining
• Bucketing: pre-hash data for repeated joins
• AQE: auto-converts shuffle→broadcast, handles skew
35 What is bucketing in Spark? Bucketing • Pre-distributes data into fixed number of files by hash
• Eliminates shuffle for joins on bucketed columns
• Both tables must be bucketed compatibly
• df.write.bucketBy(n, 'col').saveAsTable('name')
36 Spark execution flow — job to task? Execution flow • Action → DAG created → logically optimized (Catalyst)
• DAG divided into stages (at shuffle boundaries)
• Stages divided into tasks (one per partition)
• Tasks dispatched to executors via TaskScheduler
37 What is the Spark UI? What information does it show? Spark UI • Web interface for monitoring Spark applications
• Jobs tab: submitted jobs, status, duration
• Stages tab: per-stage metrics, task durations, shuffle I/O
• Executors tab: memory, CPU, task counts, GC time
38 How to debug slow Spark jobs using UI? Debug, slow • Check Stages tab for straggler tasks (data skew)
• Check shuffle read/write sizes (excessive shuffle)
• Check GC time in Executors tab (memory pressure)
• Use explain(True) to inspect physical plan
39 UDFs in PySpark — pros and cons? UDF, PySpark • User Defined Functions for custom column logic
• Con: breaks Catalyst optimization (treated as black box)
• Con: serialization overhead between JVM and Python
• Prefer: built-in Spark functions or Pandas UDFs
40 Pandas UDFs (Vectorized UDFs)? Pandas UDF, Arrow • Process data in batches as Pandas Series (not row-by-row)
• Uses Apache Arrow for efficient JVM↔Python transfer
• 10-100x faster than regular UDFs
• @pandas_udf(return_type) decorator
41 What is Apache Arrow? Why used in Spark? Arrow, serialization • In-memory columnar data format for efficient data exchange
• Eliminates serialization overhead between JVM and Python
• Used by: Pandas UDFs, toPandas(), createDataFrame(pandas_df)
• Enable: spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled=true
42 Spark Shuffle parameters to tune? Shuffle, tuning • spark.sql.shuffle.partitions: default 200, adjust per data size
• spark.shuffle.compress=true: compress shuffle data
• spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true: AQE auto-tunes shuffle
• Monitor shuffle read/write in Spark UI
43 What is predicate pushdown? Predicate pushdown • Push filter conditions closer to the data source
• Data source (Parquet, JDBC) applies filter during read
• Reduces amount of data loaded into Spark
• Catalyst optimizer applies this automatically
44 Column pruning in Spark? Column pruning • Read only the columns needed for the query
• Columnar formats (Parquet, ORC) support this natively
• Reduces I/O and memory usage significantly
• Catalyst optimizer applies this automatically
45 How to handle null values in Spark? Null, handling • df.na.fill(value): replace nulls with default
• df.na.drop(): remove rows with nulls
• F.coalesce(col1, col2): first non-null value
• F.when(F.col('x').isNull(), ...): conditional handling
46 spark-submit options — key parameters? spark-submit • --master: cluster manager (yarn, local, k8s)
• --deploy-mode: client or cluster
• --num-executors, --executor-memory, --executor-cores
• --conf spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=100
47 What is the role of Py4J in PySpark? Py4J, bridge • Python→Java bridge library enabling PySpark
• Translates Python method calls into JVM operations
• Results returned from JVM back to Python
• Adds overhead; Pandas UDFs and Arrow minimize this
48 Spark supported languages? Languages • Scala: native language, richest API
• Java: well-supported but verbose
• Python (PySpark): most popular for data science
• R (SparkR): DataFrame API for statisticians
• SQL: through Spark SQL for querying
49 Local mode vs cluster mode — differences? Local, cluster • Local: single JVM, all threads simulate executors (development)
• Cluster: distributed across many nodes (production)
• Local: master('local[*]') uses all local cores
• Cluster: provides scalability, fault tolerance, real parallelism
50 Schema inference in Spark? Schema, inference • Spark scans data to infer column types automatically
• Works with: CSV, JSON, Parquet, Avro
• inferSchema=True for CSV/JSON (scans data — slow for large files)
• Best practice: define schema manually with StructType for production

Part 7: PySpark — DataFrames, SQL & Advanced¶

DataFrame Operations Cheat Sheet¶

Operation Syntax Description
Select df.select('col1', 'col2') Choose columns
Filter df.filter(F.col('age') > 25) Row filtering
WithColumn df.withColumn('new', F.col('x')*2) Add/modify column
Rename df.withColumnRenamed('old', 'new') Rename column
Drop df.drop('col') Remove column
GroupBy df.groupBy('dept').agg(F.avg('sal')) Aggregation
OrderBy df.orderBy(F.col('sal').desc()) Sort
Distinct df.distinct() Remove duplicates
Union df1.union(df2) Combine DataFrames
Limit df.limit(10) First N rows
FillNa df.na.fill({'age': 0}) Handle nulls
DropNa df.na.drop() Remove null rows
Cast df.withColumn('age', F.col('age').cast('int')) Type conversion

Join Types¶

Join Type Keeps Syntax
Inner Matching rows only df1.join(df2, 'key', 'inner')
Left All left + matching right df1.join(df2, 'key', 'left')
Right Matching left + all right df1.join(df2, 'key', 'right')
Outer All rows from both df1.join(df2, 'key', 'outer')
Cross Cartesian product df1.crossJoin(df2)
Semi Left rows with match in right df1.join(df2, 'key', 'left_semi')
Anti Left rows WITHOUT match df1.join(df2, 'key', 'left_anti')

Window Functions¶

from pyspark.sql.window import Window

w = Window.partitionBy('dept').orderBy(F.col('salary').desc())

df.withColumn('rank', F.rank().over(w))
 .withColumn('dense_rank', F.dense_rank().over(w))
 .withColumn('row_num', F.row_number().over(w))
 .withColumn('running_sum', F.sum('salary').over(w))
 .withColumn('prev_sal', F.lag('salary', 1).over(w))
 .withColumn('next_sal', F.lead('salary', 1).over(w))

Reading/Writing Data¶

Format Read Write

Parquet spark.read.parquet('f.parquet') df.write.parquet('out/')

JDBC spark.read.jdbc(url, table, properties) df.write.jdbc(url, table, properties=p)

# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# PySpark DataFrame operations
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# Create sample data
emp_data = [
    (1, 'Alice',   'Sales',       65000),
    (2, 'Bob',     'Engineering', 85000),
    (3, 'Carol',   'Sales',       70000),
    (4, 'Dave',    'Engineering', 90000),
    (5, 'Eve',     'HR',          55000),
    (6, 'Frank',   'Engineering', 75000),
]
emp = spark.createDataFrame(emp_data, ['id', 'name', 'dept', 'salary'])

# Filter + Select
emp.filter(F.col('salary') > 70000).select('name', 'dept', 'salary').show()

# GroupBy + Aggregations
emp.groupBy('dept').agg(
    F.count('*').alias('count'),
    F.avg('salary').alias('avg_salary'),
    F.max('salary').alias('max_salary')
).orderBy('avg_salary', ascending=False).show()

# Window functions — rank within department
w = Window.partitionBy('dept').orderBy(F.col('salary').desc())
emp.withColumn('rank', F.rank().over(w)) \
   .withColumn('running_total', F.sum('salary').over(w)) \
   .show()

# ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Joins and SparkSQL
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────

# Department lookup table
dept_data = [('Sales', 'NYC'), ('Engineering', 'SF'), ('HR', 'Chicago')]
dept = spark.createDataFrame(dept_data, ['dept', 'location'])

# Inner join
emp.join(dept, 'dept', 'inner').show()

# Broadcast join (small table optimization)
emp.join(F.broadcast(dept), 'dept', 'inner').explain()  # Check plan

# SparkSQL — register views and query
emp.createOrReplaceTempView('employees')
dept.createOrReplaceTempView('departments')

spark.sql('''
    SELECT e.name, e.dept, e.salary, d.location,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.dept ORDER BY e.salary DESC) as rank
    FROM employees e
    JOIN departments d ON e.dept = d.dept
    WHERE e.salary > 60000
    ORDER BY e.dept, rank
''').show()

+-----------+---+-----+------+--------+
|       dept| id| name|salary|location|
+-----------+---+-----+------+--------+
|Engineering|  2|  Bob| 85000|      SF|
|Engineering|  4| Dave| 90000|      SF|
|Engineering|  6|Frank| 75000|      SF|
